senses.def: to purify and cleanse ritually and thus acquire a state of ritual acceptability

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to cause a state of moral purity
senses.comment: In a number of languages this phrase in James 4:8 may be expressed idiomatically as get rid of all your bad desires.

senses.def: pertaining to being without any relationship to God
pertaining to not having gone through a judicial hearing, with the implication of not having been condemned

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: one who busies himself in the affairs of others in an unwarranted manner
(in combination with numerable objects) a marker of distributive relations involving numerable objects
(an idiom, literally: up to a part, or: according to a part) a series in which each element follows in strict succession
a position within an area determined by other objects and distributed among such objects
a position in the middle of an area (either an object in the midst of other objects or an area in the middle of a larger area)
a marker of mediation
the husband of Sapphira
a Christian in Damascus
a Jewish high priest
to learn the location of something by intentional searching
to resist by actively opposing pressure or power
senses.comment: In a number of languages one may appropriately translate ‘to resist’ in a number of contexts as ‘to fight back against’ or ‘to oppose in return.’ In some contexts, however, such as Acts 7:51, the meaning may perhaps be best expressed by a negation, for example, ‘you have never been willing to yield to the Holy Spirit.’

senses.def: pertaining to a series which has no end
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘endless’ is rendered as ‘it cannot be counted’ or ‘there is never a last one.’

senses.def: to release or set free, with the implied analogy to the process of freeing a slave
senses.comment: In a number of languages one cannot speak of ‘being set free’ without specifying the particular manner or circumstances involved. In the case of Luke 24:21, for example, it may be necessary to translate ‘to liberate Israel’ as ‘to cause Israel to be free from foreign control’ or ‘… from the power of Rome.’ A similar type of translation may be required in Luke 2:38, but in the case of Ephesians 1:7 it may be necessary to specify ‘we are set free from sin’ or ‘we are set free from our bad desires.’

senses.def: one who makes objects out of silver (especially jewelry and fine utensils)
to rule or govern, with the implication of preeminent position and status
to initiate an action, process, or state of being
senses.comment: ἄρχω[b] may also be used in an absolute sense in which the related activity is merely implied: αὐτὸς ἦν Ἰησοῦς ἀρχόμενος ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα ‘when Jesus began, he was about thirty years old’ Luke 3:23. In rendering Luke 3:23, it may be useful to translate as ‘when Jesus began his ministry, he was about thirty years old.’

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End
senses.def: a point of time at the beginning of a duration
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand this expression in Acts 1:22 as ‘beginning from the time of John’s baptizing (him).’

senses.subdomain: Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
senses.def: a state of dishonor or disrespect as a negative of τιμή[a] ‘honor, respect’ (87.4)
a Roman province including the most important parts of Greece
to strongly detest something on the basis that it is abominable
senses.comment: It is possible that in Revelation 21:8 ἐβδελυγμένοις refers to sexual perverts.

senses.def: a hole, trench, or pit, natural or dug
senses.comment: In a number of languages a distinction is made between ditches dug by people for presumably agricultural purposes and those which are natural depressions in the ground. There is no way to determine from the NT contexts which type of ditch is involved.

senses.def: the state of being married
the ceremony associated with becoming married
a relatively large room, often serving as a place for a wedding
senses.comment: In Matthew 22:10 a number of manuscripts read νυμφών rather than γάμος.

senses.def: pertaining to being written

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to lure or entice someone to sin (compare δέλεαρ ‘bait,’ not occurring in the NT)
senses.comment: δελεάζω may often be translated as ‘to make sinning look attractive’ or ‘to make sin taste good’ or ‘to wave sin in front of a person’s nose.’

senses.def: (derivative of διακονέω[a] ‘to serve,’ 35.19) a person who renders service
senses.comment: In rendering θεράπων, ὑπηρέτης, and διάκονος[a] in the sense of ‘servant,’ it is important to avoid a term which would be too specific, for example, ‘one who serves meals’ or ‘one who works around the house.’ It may, in fact, be necessary to use an expression which means essentially ‘helper.’

senses.def: one who serves as a deacon, with responsibility to care for the needs of believers

senses.subdomain: Cause To Be Safe, Free from Danger
senses.def: to guard or protect something in order to keep it safe or free from harm
pertaining to being uncertain about the truth of something
(derivative of δωρέομαι ‘to give, to grant,’ 57.83) that which is given or granted
senses.comment: Since δῶρον in Matthew 5:24 refers specifically to the sacrifice, it may be useful to translate this phrase as ‘leave there your sacrifice before the altar.’

senses.def: a place for making gifts or offerings (see γαζοφυλάκιον[b] - 6.141)
senses.comment: According to tradition there were thirteen such offering boxes in the Temple and the receptacles leading down to the boxes were made in the form of trumpets. As a result, the sound of coins falling into the boxes was rather conspicuous.|In Luke 21:4 it is possible to interpret εἰς τὰ δῶρα not as ‘into the offering boxes’ but as ‘for their gifts,’ thus reflecting a more common meaning of δῶρον[a] gift (57.84).

senses.def: to make clean by removing that which is unclean
senses.comment: In 1 Corinthians 5:7 ἐκκαθαίρω is used in a complex figurative expression and may often be better rendered as ‘to get rid of’ or ‘to remove.’

senses.def: pertaining to being willing to do something without being forced or pressured
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘willingness’ to perform some action is expressed negatively, for example, ‘not having to’ or ‘not being forced to’ or ‘not being told one must.’ A positive expression of ‘willingness’ may be indicated idiomatically by a phrase such as ‘my heart approves.’

senses.def: pertaining to a speaker
extension from a source, with the point of reference near the speaker
to cause someone to live again after having once died
to cause to come into existence
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐξεγείρω in Romans 9:17, see 87.38.

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: to cause someone to have a higher position and status
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐξεγείρω in Romans 9:17, see 13.83.

senses.subdomain: Units of Time with Reference to Other Units or Points of Time: Yesterday, Today, Next Day
senses.def: a day immediately following a previous day
to speak of a person or object by means of a proper name

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to choose for a particular purpose
to acquire or gain what is sought after
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret ἐπιτυγχάνω in certain contexts as being essentially equivalent to the experiencer of an event and thus equivalent to τυγχάνω (see 90.61).

senses.def: to experience some happening (generally neutral in connotation)
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐπιτυγχάνω in Romans 11:7, see 57.60.

senses.def: to be wrongly or poorly matched in an association
senses.comment: It is often necessary to indicate somewhat more precisely the manner in which one may be wrongly matched with others. Accordingly, one can translate 2 Corinthians 6:14 as ‘do not attempt to work together with those who are unbelievers’ or ‘do not become partners with those who do not believe.’

senses.def: a hybrid formation from Greek and Latin, meaning literally either ‘east wind’ or ‘broad wind’: a strong storm wind blowing from the northeast
senses.comment: It is, of course, possible to use the form Εὐρακύλων as a proper name, but this is probably much less meaningful than employing a term such as ‘strong northeast wind’ or ‘a strong storm coming from the northeast.’ In instances in which languages do not readily and easily distinguish between north and northeast or between east and northeast, it may be satisfactory simply to use a term such as ‘east,’ but frequently one can use a designation for ‘northeast’ such as ‘between the north and the east’ or ‘a little to the north of east.’

senses.def: a Christian lawyer
to take care of, with the implication of cherishing and concern for
senses.comment: It may be useful in some instances to translate ‘and takes care of it’ in Ephesians 5:29 as ‘and gives to his own body whatever is needed’ or ‘and does for himself whatever is necessary.’

senses.def: trouble involving direct suffering
senses.comment: For a number of languages ‘trouble and suffering’ may be expressed as ‘that which causes pain.’

senses.def: pertaining to being devoted to a proper expression of religious beliefs
senses.comment: In a number of languages the concept of ‘living a godly life’ may be best expressed as ‘to live as God would have one live’ or ‘to live like one should who believes in God’ or ‘to always do what God requires.’ In some languages, however, the only equivalent is ‘to live a good life’ or ‘to live always doing good to others.’ The shift from the focus upon religious belief to good living or being good to others results from the fact that in some religious systems there is little or no connection between religious beliefs and moral behavior.

senses.def: (derivative of ἰσχύς[a] ‘capability,’ 74.8) to have special personal ability to do or experience something
to be physically strong enough for some purpose
a state of being healthy, with the implication of robustness and vigor

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: the state of being relatively recent, with the implication of being appropriately contemporary
the state of being new and different, with the implication of superiority
to cause to move down
senses.comment: This word is only found in three variant readings: ἐκ δὲ τοῦ ὄχλου κατεβίβασαν Ἀλέξανδρονπροβαλόντων αὐτὸν τῶν Ἰουδαίων ‘some of the crowd brought Alexander down, since he had been put forward by the Jews’ Acts 19:33 (apparatus); ἕως ᾅδου καταβιβασθήσω ‘you will be brought down to hell’ Matthew 11:23 (apparatus). See also Luke 10:15 (apparatus).

senses.def: to cease one’s work or activity, resulting in a period of rest
senses.comment: καταπαύω[a] and κατάπαυσις[b] (23.80) in that the emphasis of καταπαύω[a] and κατάπαυσις is more upon the cessation of activity resulting in rest rather than upon the mere restorative character of rest.

senses.def: to cause someone to cease from activity and as a result to enjoy a period of rest
to cause something or someone to cease from some activity or state
to teach in a systematic or detailed manner
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand κατηχέω in Luke 1:4 as denoting merely what has been told rather than what has been taught (see κατηχέω[b], 33.190). This distinction is an important one since it implies a quite different relationship of Theophilus to the text of the Gospel of Luke. If Luke 1:4 pertains merely to Theophilus ‘being told’ something, then one might assume that Theophilus was not a Christian, in which case he may have been a government official to whom the joint publications (the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles) would have been directed as a defense of Christianity. On the other hand, if one understands κατηχέω in the sense of ‘to be taught’ or ‘to be instructed,’ then one would assume that Theophilus was a Christian who had been instructed in the faith. The relationship of Theophilus to the message would then determine in a number of contexts the difference between ‘we’ inclusive and ‘we’ exclusive.

senses.def: to report in a relatively detailed manner
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand κατηχέω in Luke 1:4 as systematic teaching (see 33.225).

senses.def: a large box-like structure (the vessel built by Noah)
senses.comment: The central meaning of κιβωτός is ‘box’ or ‘chest,’ but it was apparently applied to Noah’s ark in view of the type of construction and the fact that Noah’s ark resembled more a barge than a seagoing vessel. However, in view of the size of Noah’s ark, it is probably best in most languages to speak of it as a ‘ship.’

senses.def: any box-like container, whether plain or elaborate; here, refers to the box used to hold the tablets of the Law
senses.comment: In the NT κιβωτός[b] occurs only in the phrase κιβωτὸς τῆς διαθήκης ‘the box of the covenant,’ which was placed in the Holy of Holies of the Temple in Jerusalem and referred to also as being in the heavenly temple (Revelation 11:19).|In the case of English some persons object to speaking of the so-called ‘ark of the Covenant’ as ‘the Covenant Box,’ since they assume that the English word ‘ark’ has some special meaning equivalent to the corresponding Greek or Hebrew terms. However, the term ‘ark’ in Old English and Middle English is simply a borrowing of Latin arca meaning ‘box, chest, coffer.’ In present-day English the term ark is known primarily from the context of ‘Noah’s ark.’

senses.def: to punish, with the implication of resulting severe suffering
senses.comment: In a number of languages punishment is often expressed as a causative of suffering, that is to say, ‘to cause to suffer’ or ‘to cause to endure harm.’ In some languages, however, there are a number of different types of punishment, and clear distinctions must be made between various degrees of punishment as well as between physical versus mental punishment.

senses.def: a companion of Paul
to receive, with the implication that the process is related somehow to divine will or favor
senses.comment: It is, however, possible to interpret λαγχάνω in Acts 1:17 and in 2 Peter 1:1 as referring to the process of divine choice and thus translate as ‘be chosen to have.’

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to choose by lot, probably by the use of marked pebbles or pieces of pottery
senses.comment: In a number of languages the closest equivalent to ‘casting lots,’ particularly for this type of context, is ‘to gamble.’

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to be selected by a decision based on the casting of lots, with the possible implication of reflecting divine choice
to kill or attempt to kill by means of hurling stones, normally carried out by angry mobs
a person noted for unusual capacity of understanding based upon astrology (such persons were regarded as combining both secular and religious aspects of knowledge and understanding)
senses.comment: In Matthew 2:1 μάγοι may be translated as ‘men of wisdom who studied the stars.’

senses.def: (derivative of μαγεύω ‘to practice magic,’ 53.96) one who practices magic and witchcraft
a relatively short sword (or even dagger) used for cutting and stabbing
senses.comment: The phrase στόμα μαχαίρης (literally ‘mouth of the sword’) refers to the event of killing or slaughter: ἔφυγον στόματα μαχαίρης ‘they escaped being killed by the sword’ Hebrews 11:34. See 79.109.

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of μάχαιρα[a] ‘sword,’ 6.33)
senses.comment: For another interpretation of μάχαιρα in Matthew 10:34, see 39.25.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of μάχαιρα[a] ‘sword,’ 6.33) death by violence or execution
(a figurative extension of meaning of μάχαιρα[a] ‘sword,’ 6.33) a state of discord and strife
senses.comment: For another interpretation of μάχαιρα in Matthew 10:34, see 55.6.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to bear the sword) to have the capacity or authority to punish
glosses: to have the power to punish

senses.def: to move away from a reference point, perhaps more definitively than in the case of πορεύομαι[c] and ἄγω[c] (15.34)
a reward or recompense, whether positive or negative, which has been granted to someone
talk which is both foolish and stupid
a large bowl, normally made of clay, used for washing of hands, face, and feet
(a figurative extension of meaning of ὀδύνη ‘physical pain,’ not occurring in the NT) a state of severe emotional anxiety and distress

to affirm the truth of a statement by calling on a divine being to execute sanctions against a person if the statement in question is not true (in the case of a deity taking an oath, his divine being is regarded as validating the statement)
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is necessary to be quite specific in referring to the swearing of an oath, for example, ‘to say something by calling upon God to listen’ or ‘to state that something is true and asking God to punish if it is not true’ or ‘to make God responsible for what one has said.’|For Mark 14:71 see 33.472.

senses.def: to demand that a person take an oath as to the truth of what is said or as to the certainty that one will carry out the request or command
glosses: to insist that one take an oath
senses.comment: It is extremely difficult to translate ὁρκίζω, ἐνορκίζω, and ἐξορκίζω in a literal manner, though in some contexts one can say ‘I put you under oath,’ but in a number of passages the person speaking is imploring and not necessarily in a position to command or insist. Therefore, in a passage such as Mark 5:7, one may render the meaning idiomatically as ‘for God’s sake, I ask you, do not punish me.’ In 1 Thessalonians 5:27 one may translate ‘in the name of the Lord, I ask you to read this letter to all the Christian brothers,’ and in Matthew 26:63 one may translate ‘in the name of the living God, I charge you, Tell us who you are.’|In most languages one may translate ὁρκίζω, ἐνορκίζω, and ἐξορκίζω by simply adding a causative component to terms meaning ‘to swear’ or ‘to take an oath.’ In other words, ὁρκίζω, ἐνορκίζω, and ἐξορκίζω may be rendered as ‘to cause a person to say under oath.’

senses.def: to come to believe something to be true and to respond accordingly, with some emphasis upon the source
to accept the presence of a person with friendliness
(an idiom, literally: to bring every effort to) to do one’s very best in attempting to do something
glosses: to try as hard as possible
senses.comment: In some languages it may be almost impossible to speak of ‘adding goodness to faith.’ However, an appropriate equivalent of this expression in 2 Peter 1:5 may be ‘do your best to be good as well as to believe.’

senses.def: to try to learn the nature or character of someone or something by submitting such to thorough and extensive testing
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand πειράζω and ἐκπειράζω in Matthew 16:1 and Luke 10:25 as meaning ‘to try to trap’ (see 27.31). See also 88.308.

senses.def: to obtain information to be used against a person by trying to cause someone to make a mistake
glosses: to attempt to catch in a mistake
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret πειράζω and ἐκπειράζω in Matthew 16:1 and Luke 10:25 as ‘the process of testing or examining’ (see 27.46). See also 88.308.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to endeavor or attempt to cause someone to sin
senses.comment: In translating expressions involving tempting or trying, it is necessary in a number of languages to indicate clearly whether or not the temptations succeeded. Therefore, it may not be sufficient in Mark 1:13 to simply say ‘Satan tempted him’; in fact, in some instances it may be necessary to make the failure of the temptation quite specific, for example, ‘Satan tried to make Jesus sin, but was not successful.’

senses.def: to attempt to do something, with the implication of not succeeding
senses.comment: In a number of languages expressions such as πειράζω[d], πειράομαι, and πεῖραν λαμβάνω may be expressed as to start to do something, but not be able to or to think that one can do something, but discover it is impossible.

senses.def: (a title for the Devil, literally: one who tempts) one who tempts or tries people with the intent of making them sin
senses.comment: A common equivalent of ὁ πειράζων is ‘one who tries to make people sin’ or ‘one who tries to cause people to sin.’

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Marking and Writing
senses.def: a flat stone on which inscriptions could be made
senses.comment: In the NT πλάξ is used to refer to the tablets of the Law given to Moses on Mount Sinai.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a person having full status as a member of a socio-political unit of people
senses.comment: In a number of languages a citizen may be described as ‘a person who belongs to that country’ or ‘one who is a part of the people of that country’ or ‘one who is counted as a person of that country,’ but one could be a citizen of a country without necessarily living in such a geographical area.|In Hebrews 8:11 (καὶ οὐ μὴ διδάξωσιν ἕκαστος τὸν πολίτην αὐτοῦ ‘none of them will have to teach his fellow citizen’) πολίτης occurs with the possessive pronoun αὐτοῦ and hence is therefore equivalent to συμπολίτης (11.72) in meaning.

senses.def: (derivative of πρεσβεία ‘representative,’ 37.87) to function as a representative of a ruling authority
senses.comment: It may be possible to render ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ οὖν πρεσβεύομεν in 2 Corinthians 5:20 as ‘we serve as those who have been delegated by Christ’ or ‘our work has been specially assigned by Christ.’

senses.def: to come to a decision beforehand
glosses: to decide upon ahead of time

senses.def: to give detailed instructions as to what must be done
to arrange in a prescribed manner
senses.comment: In some languages it may be important to recast to some extent the rendering of the second part of Acts 17:26 so as to combine both place and time, for example, ‘he set limits to the time and determined the places they would dwell.’

senses.def: pertaining to being poor and destitute, implying a continuous state
senses.comment: See comments at 57.51.|Since in all societies there are poor people, there is no difficulty involved in finding a suitable expression to designate such persons, but in some languages idiomatic phrases are used, for example, ‘those who walk in rags’ or ‘those whose ribs are always showing.’

senses.def: pertaining to being of inadequate or insufficient value
senses.comment: It is possible that πτωχός in Galatians 4:9 refers to the contrast with that which is beneficial or useful, in which case the meaning of πτωχός in this context would be classified in Subdomain D Useful, Useless (Domain 65 Value).

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: poor in spirit) pertaining to one who is humble with regard to his own capacities (in the one NT occurrence, namely, Matthew 5:3, this humility is in relationship to God)
senses.comment: A literal translation of πτωχὸς τῷ πνεύματι may lead to serious misunderstanding, since ‘poor in spirit’ is likely to mean either ‘lacking in the Holy Spirit’ or ‘lacking in ambition or drive.’ In order to indicate clearly that this poverty or need is related in some way to spiritual realities, one may translate ‘happy are those who recognize their need of God.’

senses.def: a maidservant in the house of Μαρία 6
to sweep by using a broom
a trap, probably of the type which has a stick which when touched by an animal causes the trap to shut
senses.comment: In Romans 11:9 παγίς (6.23), θήρα (6.24), and σκάνδαλον would all seem to be completely parallel in structure and meaning. As a result, in a number of languages the three terms are reduced often to two, for example, ‘snare’ and ‘trap.’ If there are three different kinds of traps, then, of course, three terms can be used. In some cases, however, it may be preferable to use verbs to express the catching and trapping, and thus one may translate γενηθήτω ἡ τράπεζα αὐτῶν εἰς παγίδα καὶ εἰς θήραν καὶ εἰς σκάνδαλον as in TEV, “may they be caught and trapped at their feasts; may they fall.”

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σκάνδαλον[a] ‘trap,’ 6.25) that which or one who causes someone to sin
glosses: that which causes someone to sin
one who causes someone to sin

senses.def: that which causes offense and thus arouses opposition
the kernel part of fruit, usually grain
senses.comment: A number of languages make distinctions between two quite different types of seed: (1) those produced by grasses (that is to say, grains) and (2) those produced by other types of plants, for example, beans, squash, apples, etc. In all passages employing the Greek terms in this subdomain (κόκκος, σπέρμα, σπόρος), it is best to use some expression referring to ‘grain.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σπέρμα[a] ‘seed,’ 3.35) posterity, with emphasis upon the ancestors role in founding the lineage
senses.comment: See discussion at 10.28.

senses.def: a derivative and imparted nature
senses.comment: If in some languages it is not possible to speak literally of ‘God’s nature,’ it may still be possible to render the second clause in 1 John 3:9 as ‘because something of what God is like is in him’ or ‘because he has in himself something of what God is like.’

senses.def: (idioms, literally: to raise up seed) the male role in begetting children
senses.comment: In contexts such as Matthew 22:24, Mark 12:19, and Luke 20:28 it may be important to add a note concerning levirate responsibilities, that is to say, the requirement for a younger brother to beget children by a deceased older brother’s wife and the reckoning of such an offspring as being the descendant of the older deceased brother.

senses.def: a large organized group of soldiers
a small detachment of soldiers
to pluck or pick by pulling off or out of, with the intent of gathering together
senses.comment: See footnote at τρυγάω 43.18.

senses.def: to cause someone else in addition to change from belief in what is true to belief in what is false
glosses: to cause to go astray together

senses.def: to associate with one another, normally involving spacial proximity and/or joint activity, and usually implying some kind of reciprocal relation or involvement
glosses: to be in the company of
senses.comment: In translating terms referring to association, one may employ a number of different kinds of expressions, for example, ‘to have something to do with,’ ‘to keep company with,’ ‘to go around with,’ ‘to join in doing things together,’ or ‘to become a companion of.’ Sometimes association is spoken of in terms of the impression made upon others, for example, ‘to be seen often together,’ ‘to be regarded as close friends,’ and even idiomatically as ‘to be another person’s shadow.’|It is also possible to interpret the phrase τοῖς ταπεινοῖς συναπαγόμενοι in Romans 12:16 as meaning ‘share in doing what is humble’ (see 41.22).

senses.def: to share in engaging continuously in some activity
senses.comment: συναπάγομαι in Romans 12:16 may also be understood as meaning ‘to involve oneself with,’ and hence one may translate ‘do not be proud, but become involved with humble people’ or ‘… make friends with humble people.’ For this interpretation, see 34.1.

senses.def: to help by joining in an activity or effort
senses.comment: In a number of instances it is not necessary to specify the joint effort or activity, since this is supplied by the context itself as, for example, in Luke 5:7 in which ‘coming to help’ indicates clearly the joint efforts. But in some languages it may be important to use a specific expression rather than a generic one. Accordingly, ‘to come and help them’ in Luke 5:7 may be rendered as ‘to come and work with them.’

senses.def: a Greek monetary unit (also a unit of weight) with a value which fluctuated, depending upon the particular monetary system which prevailed at a particular period of time (a silver talent was worth approximately six thousand denarii with gold talents worth at least thirty times that much)
senses.comment: In Matthew 25:15 what is important is the relative number of talents or sums of money. In a number of translations the respective amounts are stated in terms of local currency. For example, in English one may speak of five thousand dollars as equivalent to five talents, though in terms of buying power, five talents would be worth much more than five thousand dollars. What is important, however, in this story is not the precise sums of money but the relative amount which was given to the different servants.|The ‘ten thousand talents’ referred to in Matthew 18:24 would be equivalent to millions of denarii. The sum in this parable is perhaps greatly exaggerated, precisely in order to emphasize the vast differences between the two debts. It is also true, of course, that in ancient times persons with extensive mercantile businesses sometimes became slaves as a result of defeat in war, and they were purchased by business syndicates together with their business enterprises, which they would continue to manage.

senses.def: (derivative of τέφρα ‘ashes,’ not occurring in the NT) to destroy by reducing something to ashes
senses.comment: It is possible to render ‘to reduce to ashes’ as ‘to burn up completely’ or ‘to destroy by fire and leave only ashes.’

senses.subdomain: Once, Twice, Three Times, Etc. [Cardinals of Time]
senses.def: three occurrences
to continue to move along
to move away from a reference point, perhaps more definitively than in the case of πορεύομαι[c] and ἄγω[c] (15.34)
to depart from someone’s presence, with the implication of a changed relation
to depart from life, as a euphemistic expression for death
to undergo a significant change
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret ὑπάγω in Revelation 17:8 as ‘to experience a state’ (Domain 90M), and there may be in the context of Revelation 17:8 some aspect of movement (Domain 15).

senses.def: to resist by holding one’s ground
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ὑπομένω in James 1:12, see 68.17.

senses.def: to stay longer in a place than one is expected to
to continue in an activity or state despite resistance and opposition
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ὑπομένω in James 1:12, see 39.20.

senses.def: (derivative of ὑπομονή ‘endurance,’ 25.174) to continue to bear up despite difficulty and suffering
to bear or carry something from one place to another
to cause to move to a place, with a possible implication of assistance or firm control
to cause an object to move by means of a force
to so influence others as to cause them to follow a recommended course of action
senses.comment: In some languages it is difficult to distinguish readily between expressions for ‘leading’ and those which refer to ‘ruling’ or ‘governing,’ but it is important to try to distinguish clearly between these two different sets of interpersonal relations. In some languages, the concept of ‘leading’ can be expressed by ‘showing how to’ or ‘demonstrating how one ought to.’ In other languages it is possible to speak of ‘leading’ as simply ‘going ahead of,’ but too often such an expression may designate only ‘a scout’ who goes ahead to see whether things are safe, or it may refer only to a person who insists on his prerogative as the most distinguished person in a group.

senses.def: to be oriented in the direction of a movement
to cause something adverse to happen to someone, usually in connection with accusations or condemnations
to put or place an object by moving it to a particular point
to experience an event or state which may be burdensome or difficult
to cause to continue by sustaining or maintaining a state
senses.comment: In some languages, however, the closest equivalent of this expression in Hebrews 1:3 may be ‘causing everything to continue to be as it is by his powerful word.’|It is also possible to interpret φέρω in Hebrews 1:3 as ‘to cause to continue to exist,’ in which case it may be classified after 13.89. However, the focus seems to be on the state of being.

senses.def: to present evidence that something has actually happened
senses.comment: In rendering φέρω in Hebrews 9:16, it may be necessary to redistribute the semantic components even as in the case of the English translation, for example, ‘to show … actually …’

senses.def: to accept, but with the implication of the truth being difficult to comprehend or to respond to properly
to put up with annoyance or difficulty
to produce fruit or seed (of plants)
to produce fruit or seed (of plants)
to move from one place to another, with the possible implication of causing the movement of some other object or objects
senses.comment: It is possible that in Acts 2:2 φέρομαι should be understood in an idiomatic sense of ‘blowing,’ since it is combined with the noun for ‘wind’ (πνοή[a], 14.4). In any event, one must often translate φέρομαι[a] as ‘blowing,’ since this is frequently the appropriate type of term to use in speaking of the movement of wind.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of φέρομαι[a] ‘to move from one place to another,’ 15.11) to change from one state to another, with the implication of progressive development
to deprive a person of life by illegal, intentional killing
a particularly valuable or fine type of bronze or brass, possibly even an alloy containing some gold
senses.comment: In the two references with χαλκολίβανον in the NT (Revelation 1:15 and Revelation 2:18) the emphasis is upon the lustrous appearance of the metal. A satisfactory equivalent may be ‘bright bronze’ or ‘shining metal.’

senses.def: the sexual function or use of the same or opposite sex
senses.comment: It is often possible to refer to ‘natural sexual function’ as ‘sexual relations with the opposite sex’ or ‘men having sexual relations with women.’ ‘That which is contrary to nature’ may be expressed often as ‘men having sexual relations with men’ and ‘women having sexual relations with women.’ In many societies homosexuality is almost unknown, but there are always ways of speaking about such relations in a euphemistic manner.

senses.def: to experience pains associated with giving birth
glosses: to suffer pain in connection with giving birth

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of ὠδίνω[a] ‘to suffer birth pain,’ 23.54) to suffer intensely (similar to birth pain)
